item.title: Northflank security breach leads to abuse of customers' AI API keys
item.description: Cloud application hosting platform Northflank is warning customers to rotate all credentials and secrets stored on its platform after a security breach led to unauthorized use of customers' AI API keys. Northflank is a cloud platform that allows developers to deploy and manage applications, containers, databases, and AI applications without managing the underlying infrastructure. The company disclosed a security incident on October 30, warning customers to immediately rotate their environment variables and API keys after receiving a threat alert from cloud security company Wiz. Soon after, Northflank told all customers to assume their environment variables had been decrypted and that the secrets stored within them were stolen. "Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys," Northflank warned in an October 30 update. Applications commonly use environment variables to store sensitive information, including database passwords, cloud service credentials, authentication tokens, and API keys. If exposed, these credentials can be used to breach other customer services, potentially leading to data theft or unauthorized charges through API keys. Northflank later confirmed that multiple customers had reported unauthorized use of AI API keys stored on the platform. "Users have reported unauthorised use of AI API keys supplied to the Northflank platform," the company said. "If you have not already rotated your user-provided secrets stored in Northflank, please do so immediately." Customers were also advised to review their AI provider usage and billing logs for unexpected activity and report suspicious usage to Northflank and their AI providers. According to Northflank's published incident timeline, Wiz warned them about the breach at 11:43 UTC on October 30, which the company's engineers reviewed one minute later. Northflank quickly responded with a network policy patch, followed by additional patches at 12:50 UTC and 13:05 UTC. The company also requested assistance from Wiz's incident response team. The company has not disclosed how attackers gained access to its systems, how many customers were affected, or whether attackers stole or abused credentials other than the reported AI API keys. As part of its response, Northflank enabled credential rotation for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, and Redis. The company also enabled audit logs for all customers, including those using free accounts, to help them investigate any suspicious activity. Northflank continues to advise customers to rotate secrets stored in workloads, secret groups, and global secrets, and to disable public access to add-ons where enabled. BleepingComputer contacted Northflank with questions about the breach, its impact on customers, and whether stored credentials were accessed or stolen, but has not received a response. The breach comes amid a series of attacks targeting AI development platforms, which security researchers believe are valuable targets because they store API keys that can be used to access expensive AI services. In a report titled " Black October for AI Developer Platforms ," Wiz identified at least nine security incidents affecting AI development platforms during the month, including Northflank, Railway , OpenCode , Warp , and Lightning AI. The Railway incident also involved potential exposure of decrypted customer environment variables, while OpenCode disclosed exposed AI API keys. Warp reported a breach that exposed AI agent logs and user telemetry data. Wiz says attackers involved in some of these incidents have specifically targeted environment variables containing AI service credentials, which can be exploited through a practice known as LLMJacking . LLMJacking involves using stolen credentials to access AI models using another organization's API keys, generating massive API charges or allowing the stolen access to be resold. item.title: New Android SMS of Death exploit can remotely crash unpatched phones
item.description: A security researcher has released a proof-of-concept exploit for a recently patched Android vulnerability, dubbed "SMS of Death" and tracked as CVE-2026-58882, that lets attackers remotely disrupt cellular service or crash phones by sending a specially crafted text message. The zero-click denial-of-service flaw can interrupt ongoing calls, including emergency calls, without requiring any interaction from the target. What's worse, Android processes the message before it reaches the SMS inbox, leaving victims with no visible indication of what caused their phones to crash. According to the vulnerability researcher, Mark Blah, Google reportedly patched the vulnerability in its October 2026 Android security updates for Android 14 through 17. However, the flaw is not listed in Google's October security bulletin, and older Android 12 and 13 devices remain vulnerable because they did not receive the fix. Blah published a technical analysis of the flaw, caused by improper validation of a header-length value in Android's WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu function. To exploit the flaw, an attacker can send the following malformed eight-byte WAP Push message to targeted phones: 01 06 88 80 80 80 00 BE → sent as a data SMS to port 2948 When this value is translated into a signed 32-bit integer without a bounds check, it becomes -2147483648. When Android attempts to allocate memory using this negative value, it triggers a NegativeArraySizeException that crashes the com.android.phone process. As the com.android.phone process manages cellular functions, the crash disrupts mobile connectivity and disconnects ongoing phone calls, including calls to emergency services. The researcher says the attack can also cause repeated crashes when carriers attempt to redeliver malicious messages or Android tries to process messages already stored on the phone. When testing the flaw, the researcher found that sending 20 malicious messages could cause phones to get stuck in reboot loops. On one Android 12 device, the phone rebooted into recovery mode approximately every 90 seconds, requiring the user to perform a factory reset to recover. A GitHub contributor named Sakis discovered a way to remove the malicious messages using Android Debug Bridge (ADB), but the process requires more advanced technical knowledge and access to a computer. The researcher has published a proof-of-concept exploit that can send the malicious messages from another Android device. Google's fix, titled "Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu," prevents the crashes by catching exceptions triggered when Android processes the malformed text messages. The patch also deletes malicious messages from the SMS database to prevent them from triggering repeated crashes. Android security updates are generally installed automatically on supported devices, but their availability depends on the device manufacturer and carrier, and a restart may be required to complete installation. Now that a working proof-of-concept exploit has been released, Android users are strongly advised to install the latest security updates to protect their devices. item.title: Reddit to lock content behind logins to fight scrapers
item.description: Reddit announced in a post by co-founder Steve Huffman that the site will gradually become a "logged-in service," offering limited access to visitors without accounts. For the past 20 years, the discussion platform has let users browse almost all its content without logging in, but according to Huffman, Reddit has now grown to a size where this is no longer sustainable. The two main points for this upcoming change are the need to offer users more personalization and to address the increasing problem of content scrapers. To tackle this, a new pilot test will begin in selected markets outside the United States in the coming months, requiring users to log in to access the site's full content. However, what content will be restricted, what countries will be impacted first, and rollout timelines have not been determined at this time. Huffman said they currently believe it's important to keep the front page accessible to all, and allow people arriving from search results or other external sources to see at least the page the URL points to. With users logged in, Reddit expects to gather more data from upvotes to help users find relevant content, join communities, and participate in discussions. "Our goal is to help you find what's most relevant to you and drive the community, connection and belonging that makes Reddit, reddit," explained Huffman . "This change will do that, helping surface what's most relevant to you and quickly getting you to where you want to go—whether that's your favorite subreddit, a game you want to play, or a thread you're looking for." More logged-in users will also let Reddit deliver more relevant ads to each member, supporting the platform's revenue stream. One of the bigger problems this change is meant to address is content scraping. Reddit says most unauthorized data access happens through its logged-out pages, so limiting access will help on that front. For AI platforms and search engines that want access to the data, Reddit will continue to license it under commercial agreements. For those concerned about privacy, Huffman said they will not require users to submit their real names or identification documents. To further strengthen privacy on the platform, Reddit will also re-release a read-only incognito mode in its app. Users will also be able to opt out of personalized advertising, which will presumably disable some internal tracking and profiling. item.title: From Beginner to Bug Hunter: Learning Cybersecurity in the AI Era.
item.description: Finding a real security flaw and getting paid for it is an appealing goal when you are learning cyber security. Bug bounties give you a chance to test your skills on real software and help its developers make it safer. Headlines about programs closing or pausing under a flood of AI reports can make that route feel less certain. Earlier this year, curl, the widely used data transfer tool and library, ended its paid bounty program after similar problems . As a beginner, these decisions raise a practical question about where to put your effort. A useful starting point is understanding what went wrong, then building the skills to produce findings that someone else can verify. A bug bounty program rewards eligible security findings under a defined set of rules. Developers must still review each submission, reproduce the issue and assess its impact. A convincing report about an imaginary vulnerability can consume time that a small security team needs for genuine problems. When curl ended its program on January 31, 2026, maintainer Daniel Stenberg explained how the quality of submissions had deteriorated. He confirmed vulnerabilities fell from above 15% in previous years to below 5% starting in 2025. Across its lifetime, the program had helped uncover 87 confirmed vulnerabilities and paid researchers more than $100,000. Those figures describe curl's experience specifically. Google's pause also has a defined scope: supply chain submissions and outstanding reports remain unaffected. Its wider vulnerability rewards programs paid researchers $17.1 million in 2025. The closures and restrictions show pressure on particular programs, while other opportunities continue. TryHackMe gives you browser-based labs and guided learning paths for every level, from complete beginner to advanced practitioner. Join 8 million+ learners and start free, with no setup needed. In April, Stenberg reported that submission quality had improved and the share of confirmed vulnerabilities had returned to roughly 15% to 16%. He observed extensive AI use in those reports. Researchers were finding real problems, although the growing volume still created work for maintainers. For someone learning, the lesson is to take responsibility for the evidence behind a finding. Generating a report is easy compared with establishing whether its claim holds up. Before chasing your first payout, learn how the systems you plan to test work. For web security, that means understanding HTTP requests, login sessions, permissions and how applications handle data. Basic networking and command line skills help you investigate what is happening when a tool produces an unexpected result. Practise these ideas in an environment designed for learning. You can make mistakes, repeat a test and inspect the result without affecting a live service. Choose a specific skill for each session, such as explaining a request or identifying which account is allowed to access a resource. TryHackMe's Cyber Security 101 learning path covers networking, Linux and Windows fundamentals, web application basics, and offensive and defensive security. Working through a structured path gives each new tool a purpose and helps you understand the evidence it produces. After a lab, write down what you changed, what happened and why. Then repeat the task with your notes closed. Being able to explain and reproduce the result is a useful way to check your progress. AI can help explain an unfamiliar error, suggest questions to investigate or review the clarity of your notes. You will get more useful practice if you attempt the task first and give the model a specific point of confusion. After inspecting a lab request, for example, ask the model to explain how the session cookie relates to the logged-in account. If you are stuck, ask for one hint and describe what you have already tried. Then test your next step and explain why it worked. Finish the session by doing the task again without assistance. item.title: Chainalysis discloses data breach from "offensive agentic techniques"
item.description: Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis has disclosed a security incident after attackers used what it describes as "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its internal systems and tools. The company says some customer information was accessed, including names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels, but claims there is no evidence that sensitive investigation data or authentication credentials were exposed. Chainalysis provides blockchain analytics tools used by law enforcement, government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, and financial institutions to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering. On Friday, roughly 5:14 PM ET, Chainalysis published a security incident disclosure along with the full text of the email sent to affected customers. The disclosure says the company detected an external actor using "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools earlier this month, and has since been patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems. The accessed data includes user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels for users provisioned on the platform. Chainalysis is still determining which records were accessed for each organization and will provide a detailed breakdown once that analysis is complete. A Chainalysis spokesperson confirmed the incident to BleepingComputer and said the company is working with external cybersecurity experts. It is also using large language models (LLMs) to support a broader security review of its platform. "Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens," the company said, adding that the incident is unrelated to the recent Binance theft. Customers are advised to enable two-factor authentication (2FA) and watch for unexpected password reset requests, authentication prompts, and scammers impersonating Chainalysis, particularly those offering fund recovery or recruiting services. Chainalysis has not shared technical details about the intrusion, including which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were accessed, or how long the attackers had access. It is unclear whether the attackers used existing agentic offensive security frameworks, such as ARTEX, or custom-built AI agents capable of autonomously identifying vulnerabilities, exploiting them, and chaining together subsequent actions. ARTEX has recently been used by threat actors, including in the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, according to Microsoft . The term "agentic" generally describes AI systems capable of executing multi-step tasks with limited human intervention, potentially allowing attackers to automate portions of the intrusion process rather than relying on traditional hands-on exploitation. The Chainalysis disclosure comes amid a relentless week of security incidents affecting the cryptocurrency and technology industries. On Friday, Binance linked the roughly $6.3 billion theft, now the largest crypto heist on record and attributed to North Korean state-backed hackers, to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. Separately, hardware wallet maker Trezor warned of a suspected cryptocurrency-stealing implant reported in a Trezor Safe 5 device sold by a Southeast Asian reseller. The implant can reportedly read the recovery phrase shown on the device's screen and transmit it over a mobile network. Meanwhile, a malicious version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through the Cursor extension marketplace, planting persistent SSH backdoors on developers' machines. Chainalysis says it will share further updates with affected customers as its investigation progresses. item.title: Critical Linux kernel flaw allows remote root attacks on MPTCP servers
item.description: Security researchers at Anthropic have developed an exploit for a critical Linux kernel vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute commands as root on servers running Multipath TCP (MPTCP) listeners. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-98432 , also affects ordinary TCP connections, although remote code execution has not been publicly demonstrated on servers without an MPTCP listener. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is a TCP feature that lets a single connection use multiple network paths at the same time to improve performance and reliability. It is commonly used in environments where devices have multiple network connections, such as Wi-Fi and cellular networks. CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free vulnerability in the kernel's IPv4 TCP networking code that received a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 from the Linux kernel CVE team. The vulnerability affects Linux kernels dating back to version 4.4, including widely used distributions such as Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), and Rocky Linux. According to the Linux kernel advisory , the vulnerability stems from a race condition in how the kernel handles TCP connection requests, potentially causing a use-after-free condition. "tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it," reads the advisory. "Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req(). tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice." A similar issue can occur during TCP request socket migration when net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req is enabled, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program is used. Although triggering the vulnerability requires no authentication, Red Hat says exploiting the race condition is more complex than just sending a malicious network packet. Red Hat classifies the vulnerability as a potential denial-of-service issue that could cause a kernel crash, assigning it a lower severity score of 5.9 because exploitation is complex. However, researchers at Anthropic demonstrated that the vulnerability could be exploited for remote code execution under specific conditions. An Anthropic report explained that an unreleased Claude AI model developed an exploit that bypassed kernel address space layout randomization (KASLR) and executed arbitrary commands as root on a Linux server running an MPTCP listener. According to Anthropic, the exploit took about 53 minutes to achieve remote root code execution, showing the vulnerability could be exploited for more than denial-of-service attacks. While MPTCP is not typically enabled by default in applications, some software enables it automatically. Beginning in Go 1.24, the programming language enables MPTCP by default for TCP listeners on Linux as long as the kernel supports the feature. Due to this, some Go-based network services may enable MPTCP listeners without administrators knowing. The vulnerability was fixed in the upstream Linux kernel and backported to maintained kernel branches. However, security updates have not yet been pushed out to all affected Linux distributions. According to Canonical's security tracker , Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, 26.04 LTS, and 26.10 remain vulnerable, with kernel fixes in progress as of October 30. Red Hat also lists RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected, with fixes planned for future updates. RHEL 7 is not affected because its kernel does not contain the vulnerable code. In mitigation guidance , Rocky Linux support provider CIQ confirms Rocky Linux 8, 9, and 10 are also affected and shared temporary firewall protections for affected systems. According to Debian's security tracker , the vulnerability was fixed in kernel package version 6.1.190-1 for Debian 12 (Bookworm) and 6.12.113-1 for Debian 13 (Trixie). item.title: Trezor warns of suspected crypto-theft implant in hardware wallet
item.description: Hardware wallet device maker Trezor has received credible reports about a suspected hardware crypto-theft implant in a Trezor Safe 5 sold by its reseller CryptoBilis in Southeast Asia. Although the company has not yet received the device to examine it and confirm whether there is a malicious implant, it has warned potentially affected users to move their private keys and digital assets to known safe wallets. Trezor wallets are physical devices that store cryptocurrency private keys and authorize transactions. Safe 5 is one of its latest models and is currently available for purchase from the official store. According to Trezor, the concerns arose after it received a report from an Indonesian user who purchased a Safe 5 device from CryptoBilis through Tokopedia in August 2026. The user opened it and found an extra circuit board between the wallet's main board and screen, equipped with a cellular module and antenna. Based on unconfirmed information supplied by that customer, the implant appears capable of reading information displayed on the screen, including the wallet recovery phrase, and transmitting it over a mobile network when plugged in. CryptoBilis is the same retailer implicated in a Ledger implant incident that unfolded earlier this month, and the implants on the two devices appear to be similar in form and function. Ledger later confirmed the compromise and asked resellers and distributors in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to halt all sales until the investigation confirms their safety. In response to the Ledger incident, and before it had any indication it was impacted, Trezor immediately stopped device sales through CryptoBilis on October 9, 2026. The company later announced it would restructure and tighten its reseller network globally to maintain higher levels of security. Trezor says it is unaware of any funds being stolen as a result of a supply-chain attack, and promised to provide updates once it receives the device, which is currently being shipped to it. Meanwhile, multiple reports of losses by Ledger users have emerged since earlier this month, and a recent Singapore police announcement added another $3,500,000 to the tally. For now, Trezor recommends not setting up or using any device bought via CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward. Users who have already done so are advised to move their funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase. Buyers holding proof of purchase may contact Trezor for a replacement device or a voucher for a new device. Trezor underlined that weighing devices is not a reliable way to determine if they have been tampered with. item.title: Malicious Claude Code extension on Cursor planted SSH backdoors
item.description: A malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code VS Code extension was distributed through Cursor's extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29, exposing up to 5,000 developers to malware designed to install persistent SSH backdoors. The extension used the version number 2.1.313 and was distributed between 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. Pacific Time. Cursor is an AI-powered code editor built from Microsoft's open-source Visual Studio Code (VS Code), with support for VS Code extensions. Anthropic's Claude Code extension brings its AI coding assistant directly into compatible editors, helping developers write and debug code using natural-language instructions. Cursor says Anthropic did not develop the malicious extension but has not explained how attackers distributed the compromised package under Anthropic's name. "Between about 2:27 am PT and 1:35 pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code extension Marketplace," warned Cursor . "The extension runs malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor." Researchers at Phorion and OpenSourceMalware found that the attackers inserted a malicious JavaScript loader at the beginning of the extension's extension.js file, leaving the legitimate extension code otherwise unchanged. The malicious code executes when the extension loads, without requiring user interaction with Claude Code. When installed, the malicious extension performs the following actions on compromised systems: However, according to Phorion, coding errors in the malware's SSH setup routines likely prevented attackers from gaining remote access to many affected Windows and macOS systems. The mistakes prevented the malware from enabling SSH on machines where it was not already running, leaving the reverse tunnel unable to provide access to the compromised device. On macOS, the malware attempts to check whether Remote Login is enabled using the systemsetup -getremotelogin command, but runs it without elevated privileges. Instead of returning the SSH service's status, the command produces an administrator-access error. Because the malware only attempts to enable SSH when the output contains "Off," it skips the activation step entirely. On Windows, the malware attempts to install and start the OpenSSH server through PowerShell, but it tries to do so via /bin/sh, a Unix shell that isn't available on standard Windows installations. Due to this, the SSH setup fails. In both cases, the malware can still install its SSH keys, establish persistence, and attempt to create the reverse tunnel. However, if the SSH server is not already running, the tunnel cannot provide access to the compromised machine. Even if the SSH backdoor fails, the malware still sends reconnaissance data to the attacker's server, including the victim's username, hostname, public IP address, Git email address, and names of environment variables associated with sensitive credentials. However, the script does not directly steal credentials, suggesting the attackers intended to retrieve sensitive data manually after gaining access through the SSH tunnel. Cursor removed the malicious extension and temporarily shut down its entire marketplace to audit other extensions and rotate all access keys before making it available again. The company also worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker's server offline, disrupting both the reverse SSH connections and the transmission of reconnaissance data. Following an internal investigation, Cursor says it found no evidence that any other extension versions or the official distribution were affected. Those who have downloaded the package during the exposure window should check for the presence of an 'svc-telemetry' SSH key on their machines, and follow Cursor's remediation instructions if impact is confirmed. item.title: SS7 and Diameter Attacks: How Signaling Flaws Expose Your Phone
item.description: SS7 and Diameter signaling attacks can track, intercept, and impersonate you. Here's how they work and how to stop them. Your phone can be tracked, your SMS two-factor codes can be intercepted, and your number can be impersonated, all without malware, a phishing link, or any access to your device. The attacks happen inside the telecom network, in the carrier-to-carrier control protocols known as signaling, the automated descendants of the old telephone switchboard. Most users never see them, and most carriers can't reliably stop them. Signaling attacks aren't new. Most recently, they made headlines when Iranian-linked actors reportedly exploited outdated network technology to locate the phones of US personnel in the Middle East during the Iran war. But the vulnerability has been around for decades, and it's been used for far more everyday crimes, like intercepting bank one-time passcodes. It has even been demonstrated by popular YouTubers: Veritasium hijacked a tech influencer's calls and texts using only his phone number. Criminals have reportedly exploited signaling protocols in attacks on bank accounts and global telecom infrastructure. Citizen Lab exposed two long-running commercial surveillance campaigns abusing SS7 and Diameter, with thousands of attacks against targets in dozens of countries. Congressman Ted Lieu's phone was hacked on live TV via SS7 on 60 Minutes Australia Attackers have intercepted SMS one-time passcodes to drain victims' bank accounts. Every call, text, and mobile data session requires your carrier to verify you're a paying customer and route your traffic to the right destination. Carriers do this with signaling–background messages that identify your location and forward traffic accordingly. Signaling has been the connective tissue between global providers for decades, and it is one of the most overlooked attack surfaces in mobile security. Two protocols do most of the work: SS7 (from the 1970s, used in 2G/3G) and Diameter (its successor, used in 4G and most 5G). Both were designed when a small number of large operators could plug into the system, so they assume that traffic claiming to come from a legitimate operator really does. SS7 has essentially no process for authenticating the machine making a request. Diameter supports stronger authentication on paper, but operators don't always deploy basic protections like encryption, and many fall back on the same peer-to-peer trust model. An attacker with access to the global signaling backbone, through a commercial leasing arrangement or a compromised operator, can send messages that carriers worldwide treat as trustworthy. Signaling lets an attacker ask your carrier questions and make claims on your behalf: Harvest your IMSI. Knowing your number, an attacker can request your International Mobile Subscriber ID (IMSI) under the pretense of routing a call or SMS. It can be reused for follow-on attacks for years. Locate you in real time. Queries can return the cell tower you last connected to. Others, normally reserved for emergency responders, can return the actual coordinates your phone reports. Intercept communications. The attacker claims you've roamed onto another network, so your calls and texts are redirected to them. Combined with a stolen username and password, this delivers your SMS second factor to the attacker instead of you. Impersonate or block you. With your IMSI, an attacker can place calls or send SMS as you. A false roaming claim can also cut off service to your phone. Disrupt networks. Deliberately misconfigured signaling messages can overwhelm provider systems. None of this touches your device. It happens in automated transactions you can't see and that leave no trace on your phone. Carrier signaling firewalls reliably block messages sent to or from the wrong place. item.title: CISA says max severity GitLab flaw now exploited in the wild
item.description: Attackers have started exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability patched earlier this month, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Tracked as CVE-2026-97229 , this critical security flaw was discovered by a security researcher using the ' joaxcar ' handle in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler, which parses, compiles, and evaluates regular expressions in pipeline configuration files. CVE-2026-97229 stems from an integer overflow weakness and could let remote attackers run arbitrary code on targeted instances via a maliciously crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient expression validation. "GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation," it said . GitLab addressed the security issue in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 and urged admins to patch their servers immediately. The company has also released threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances after detecting exploitation attempts. On Thursday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed active exploitation and added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog . CISA also ordered federal agencies to secure their servers by Sunday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. Although BOD 26-04 targets only federal agencies, the cybersecurity agency encouraged all security teams, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patching this flaw to protect their networks against ongoing attacks. Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver tracks nearly 2,800 Internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances , but it doesn't say how many have already been secured against attacks. ​CVE-2026-97229 is the latest in a string of security issues GitLab has addressed since the start of the year. In January, it patched a high-severity two-factor authentication bypass (CVE-2026-0723) that lets attackers who know the target's account ID circumvent two-factor authentication. Earlier this month, it fixed another maximum-severity Regular Expression Compiler flaw (CVE-2026-110264) that could let remote attackers run arbitrary code on targeted instances. In September, GitLab also addressed another maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-85706) in the repository commits API that can be abused to read sensitive data, such as credentials and other secrets, from vulnerable servers. One day later, CISA added CVE-2026-85706 to its list of actively exploited flaws after cybersecurity firm watchTowr reported that attackers had already begun scanning the Internet for unpatched GitLab servers. CISA has tagged six GitLab vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021, including two (tracked as CVE-2021-22175 and CVE-2021-39935) in February this year. GitLab's DevSecOps platform is used by over 50% of Fortune 100 companies and has more than 70 million registered users worldwide. item.title: Drupal warns of critical Commerce Core flaw exploited in attacks
item.description: Drupal warned admins to patch a critical access bypass vulnerability in the Commerce Core module that attackers are exploiting in the wild. Tracked as CVE-2026-118539 , this flaw stems from a missing authorization weakness that can be abused by unauthenticated attackers and affects Commerce Core versions 0.0.0 through 2.41 and 3.0.0 through 3.3.13. The Drupal security team asked admins on the 3.x branch to upgrade immediately to Commerce Core 3.3.13 (or Commerce Core 8.x-2.41 for earlier versions) and audit orders for inconsistencies, since threat actors are exploiting this vulnerability in attacks. "This module enables you to sell goods and services to customers through an included shopping cart and checkout form or through decoupled applications via APIs," Drupal said in a Wednesday advisory tagged as highly critical. "The module doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor. This vulnerability is being actively exploited in the wild." Commerce Core is a community-developed Drupal module used by more than 42,000 websites , including many high-profile organizations such as Fortune 500 companies and research universities. The module provides a software framework for building and running e-commerce sites and shopping apps on top of the Drupal Content Management System (CMS). In May, Drupal also warned that attackers were exploiting an SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-9082) in the database abstraction API that could lead to privilege escalation, information disclosure, and remote code execution. Days later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered federal agencies to patch their systems within three days. Two weeks ago, Drupal patched two more remote code execution security issues (CVE-2026-108097 and CVE-2026-108099) that could allow threat actors to execute code remotely, and urged admins to apply updates as soon as possible because attackers could develop exploits "within hours or days." Over the last several years, CISA has flagged 5 Drupal vulnerabilities exploited in the wild, two of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs. item.title: Binance links $6.3 billion crypto theft to compromised DevOps laptop
item.description: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has linked the theft of about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency to a DevOps engineer's compromised laptop. The crypto exchange said the access let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions after they accessed a service container, and it hasn't yet found evidence of a leaked wallet private key. "To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual," Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said . Binance also said it "uncovered additional points of breach" but was "still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." The company confirmed the breach in a statement shared with BleepingComputer on Thursday and reassured customers that their funds were safe. "Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company's funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete," it said . Since the attack, Binance has suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks, revoked authorizations for the affected address, and is working with blockchain intelligence partners and law enforcement to trace and recover the stolen funds. Although the company didn't link the incident to a hacking group or threat actor, blockchain analysis firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-backed hacking unit also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38 . "On October 29, 2026, an attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC. That makes this the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the USD 1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025," TRM said . Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis confirmed TRM Labs' findings , stating with "a high degree of confidence" that TraderTraitor is responsible for the Binance $6.4 billion hack. While stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle, Ripple, and others have frozen roughly $2.7 billion since the incident, the attackers still have control of about $2.4 billion that can't be frozen. "Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about USD 2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly USD 2.7 billion," TRM added. "The attacker raced the freezes by selling USDT to market makers and borrowing ETH against USDT on Aave. It now holds more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about USD 2.4 billion in assets beyond any issuer's reach." The TraderTraitor hackers were previously linked to many other major crypto theft incidents, including the theft of $1.5 billion in the February 2025 Bybit hack . At $6.36 billion, the Binance attack is now the largest recorded crypto heist. item.title: Binance probes potential $5.8 billion crypto-theft hack
item.description: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance is investigating a potential security breach involving up to $5.8 billion in digital assets, in what could become the largest cryptocurrency hack in history. If confirmed stolen, the amount would far exceed the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit by North Korean hackers in February 2025, the largest confirmed crypto heist on record. The suspected breach has already prompted stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle to freeze more than $2.3 billion in assets associated with the incident. In a statement to BleepingComputer, a Binance spokesperson confirmed that the exchange was investigating reports of a potential security issue while reassuring customers that their funds were safe. "Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating. Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," the spokesperson told BleepingComputer. "Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information." Binance also warned customers to remain cautious of scams and avoid unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) said on X that the incident appeared to be a hack, while noting that he no longer manages the exchange and expects all user funds to be fully covered. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company had frozen more than $1.567 billion in USDT associated with the potential Binance hack. Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire also confirmed that the company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC linked to the incident, adding that Circle was coordinating with law enforcement and would continue supporting the investigation. The statements follow reports of billions of dollars in cryptocurrency being transferred from multiple Binance hot wallets to a newly created Ethereum address. According to blockchain transaction analysis shared on X by crypto journalist StarPlatinum, a Binance hot wallet known as "Binance 14" transferred approximately $2.53 billion across 64 cryptocurrency tokens, followed 24 seconds later by another $174.4 million from a second Binance wallet. A later update claimed that a third Binance hot wallet transferred another 780 million USDC to the same Ethereum address , bringing the reported total to approximately $3.48 billion. Meanwhile, blockchain intelligence platform Arkham Intelligence is tracking 55 cryptocurrency addresses under an entity labeled "binance-hacker-1029," with combined holdings valued at approximately $5.78 billion. The tracked assets include approximately $1.77 billion in USDT, $1.44 billion in Bitcoin, $876 million in Ethereum, and $823 million in USDC. Blockchain explorer Etherscan has also labeled the initial receiving address as "Binance Hot Wallet Exploiter 2," assigning it both "Exploit" and "Heist" tags. However, it should be noted that Arkham's $5.78 billion figure is the value of assets held across all tracked wallets, rather than a confirmed amount stolen from Binance. Binance has not yet confirmed whether the transfers were unauthorized, how the suspected breach occurred, or the total value of any stolen assets. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available. item.title: Hugging Face malware campaign returns to hijack GPUs for crypto mining
item.description: A cryptomining and backdoor campaign that abuses Hugging Face model repositories came back within days of being taken down. Its most popular malicious model was downloaded more than 28,000 times. Separately, researchers flagged a fake Solana starter kit on GitHub, live since late 2025, that is positioned to trick AI coding agents into installing a remote access trojan. Researchers at Pluto Security found 31 malicious repositories across seven Hugging Face accounts, published in two waves since September. The models pose as small Qwen2 test checkpoints. They target GPU hosts running self-hosted inference servers such as Xinference and GPUStack . With linked models included, the repositories have more than 32,000 downloads. Pluto notes that this counts downloads, not confirmed infections. Instead of using poisoned weights or pickle exploits, the campaign abuses a Hugging Face option, trust_remote_code , that lets a model ship its own Python code. When a user enables it, that code runs on their machine as soon as the model loads. The most downloaded model, MENXIANGYU/qwen2-tiny , contained no actual model at all. Its code quietly installs a cryptocurrency miner disguised as a Linux system process, restarts it if killed, and removes competing miners from the machine. Some versions also open a reverse shell, giving the attacker direct access to the infected server. Pluto found the campaign through a test account whose leftover backup files pointed to the attacker's main accounts. It reported the first wave to Hugging Face and China's ModelScope, and both removed the accounts. A second wave of 19 repositories appeared under new accounts within days. Hours after Pluto reported it, the operator published another model with a script that can break out of a container and take over the server underneath. Pluto says the second-wave repositories were still live eight days after it reported them. Downloads of the flagship model climbed from 7,354 at the time of the report to 28,412 by October 28. As of writing, Hugging Face has disabled access to that model. A near-identical copy uploaded on October 25 by a newer account, htt0118 , is still live, and BleepingComputer confirmed it contains the same miner and reverse shell: Hugging Face scans uploads with antivirus and partner tools from Protect AI and JFrog. Pluto says these look for known malware and unsafe model formats, rather than what a model's Python code actually does. "The second-wave flagship scanned clean while it collected 28,412 downloads," the researchers said, adding that JFrog reported the payload file was "not a machine-learning model." According to Pluto, the operator's main wallet has received roughly $5,000 in Pearl (PRL) cryptocurrency. It was still active on mining pools after the repositories behind it were removed. While the researchers watched, nine machines that appear to belong to a shared research GPU cluster started mining for the operator at once. They dropped off about six minutes later, which Pluto says fits an admin killing the jobs. Pluto attributes the campaign to a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking operator. It cites Simplified Chinese code comments, command-and-control servers on Alibaba Cloud, and activity times that fall late at night in China. Anyone who loaded these models with trust_remote_code enabled should treat the machine as compromised, check it against the indicators in Pluto's report, and rotate any credentials it could reach. Killing the miner alone doesn't remove the backdoors. In a separate report, Air Security describes a GitHub repository, SolanaUpdateTools/solana-starter-kit , that it says ranks as the top result when AI coding agents search for a Solana starter kit. An agent that picks the repository and follows its README could run the attacker's command without the developer ever seeing it. The repository was created in November 2025 and has 286 stars. Its README promises a full Solana app template, but none of that code exists

item.title: Japan Airlines suffers third-party data breach exposing passenger info
item.description: Japan Airlines (JAL) has announced that a data breach at Amadeus's Passenger Service System exposed the data of about 92,000 customers. JAL Group, which operates the airlines JAL and Japan Transocean Air, uses the system to handle passenger reservations, ticketing, and check-in. According to its announcement , Amadeus notified the airline on October 23, 2026, that unauthorized access to its systems occurred between August 10, 2023, and September 23, 2026. As a result of this lengthy breach, the threat actor accessed reservation codes (PNRs), names, flight dates, routes, and travel classes for approximately 90,000 customers. An additional 2,000 customers had the above data types exposed, plus their email addresses, phone numbers, passport numbers, nationalities, frequent flyer numbers, and flight, ticket, and seat numbers. JAL says credit card numbers and passwords were not compromised, and assured that it currently has no evidence of customer information being misused. The company said Amadeus has now implemented the necessary security measures and flight operations are unaffected. Amadeus is an IT firm that provides solutions for travel agencies, airlines, airports, and hotels. It is a major tech supplier to global aviation, used by over four hundred airlines , 210 airport operators, 34 cruise and ferry lines, and 2 million hotels. Amadeus published a statement on its website on October 1, 2026, announcing it had discovered a vulnerability in its travel booking display environment that could expose travelers' data. At the time, the company said ransomware actors had not exploited the flaw and assured that no payment or other financial data had been exposed. As JAL has confirmed now, the vulnerability appears to have been maliciously exploited. It appears they were not the only victim of the campaign. All Nippon Airways (ANA) has also announced a customer data breach earlier today tied to Amadeus, according to local media . The airline has also suspended certain related services on its website and mobile app since October 21, although that action appears linked to the PHP2Shell threat rather than the Amadeus incident. Other airlines that have confirmed impact from the Amadeus flaw are Asiana Airlines and Korean Air , both major South Korean carriers. BleepingComputer has asked Amadeus for more information about the scope of the impact, specifically whether more airlines and other countries/markets were affected, but the company has not provided more information as of publication. item.title: Polymarket halts trading after crypto-draining script breach, $2.5M traced
item.description: Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading on Thursday after hackers compromised a third-party service to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript, with approximately $2.5 million in assets traced to a suspected attacker wallet. The company confirmed the security incident, saying it had identified and fixed the issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com, and referred the breach to law enforcement. "One of our third party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement," Polymarket said . "Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading and are working to bring the platform back online." Polymarket initially placed its exchange into cancel-only mode at 2:05 p.m. ET and paused relayer actions while investigating the incident. At 2:37 p.m., the company announced that the issue had been fixed and that trading was temporarily halted out of an abundance of caution. Trading resumed approximately one hour after the initial suspension, with the incident marked resolved at 3:05 p.m. ET. "Trading is now fully back online," the company announced on X . "We'll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders." Polymarket has not disclosed how many users were affected, how much cryptocurrency was stolen, or how the reimbursement process will work. Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified a suspected attacker-controlled wallet ( 0x3F99139F1C5854bb628c2e576Aaf638e99dFfc18 ) embedded in the malicious JavaScript. BleepingComputer's examination of the wallet's blockchain activity found that it transferred approximately 28.6 million POL, valued at roughly $2.57 million, to three additional wallets. Blockchain records also show that the wallet conducted numerous transactions involving Polymarket's prediction-market token contract between 1:50 p.m. and 1:56 p.m. ET, shortly before the exchange suspended trading. Hudson Rock reported that the wallet held approximately $2.19 million in cryptocurrency at the time of its investigation. Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified malicious JavaScript distributed through cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js that was designed to steal cryptocurrency and prediction-market holdings from Polymarket users. The script was hosted on infrastructure belonging to DebugBear, a website performance-monitoring service that helps organizations track website loading speeds and user experience. DebugBear's Real User Monitoring (RUM) service uses JavaScript embedded in websites to collect performance metrics from visitors' browsers. DebugBear has since confirmed that it is investigating an ongoing security incident and warned customers to remove its monitoring JavaScript from their websites. "We're impacted by an ongoing security incident," DebugBear said in a post on X . "If you use our RUM product, please remove the embed code from your website." At the time of writing, DebugBear's website was inaccessible, displaying a Cloudflare error. It is unclear whether the website outage is related to containment efforts or another consequence of the incident. Hudson Rock's researchers also discovered Polymarket production build metadata containing the commit message, " chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337) ," indicating that the platform had removed the DebugBear monitoring integration. The build was timestamped October 29 at 1:59 p.m. ET, shortly before Polymarket publicly announced the incident. BleepingComputer analyzed a copy of the malicious JavaScript file ( VirusTotal ), finding that it was designed to hijack authenticated Polymarket trading sessions, liquidate users' prediction-market positions, and transfer cryptocurrency and other assets to an attacker-controlled wallet. item.title: Fake crypto app on Apple App Store linked to $23K wallet theft
item.description: A fake cryptocurrency trading app called Padre Terminal, previously available on the Apple App Store for iOS devices, has been linked to the theft of approximately $23,000 from 27 Solana wallets. Blockchain investigator Iris confirmed that one victim was compromised through the malicious App Store app, but has not determined how the other affected wallets were compromised. The researcher says the app drains wallets after unsuspecting users import their private keys into it. Padre was a cryptocurrency trading platform, mainly used to buy and sell meme coins on Solana. It was later renamed Terminal by pump.fun, a platform focused on creating, buying, and selling cryptocurrency "meme coins" on the Solana blockchain. Iris says the legitimate Padre trading service, now Terminal by pump.fun, is web-only, so any mobile apps impersonating it, including the one previously available on the App Store, are malicious. At the time of BleepingComputer's initial investigation, we found two Padre apps on the App Store (ID 6802739263 and ID 6717572591). The former was the Iris-confirmed drainer app, while the latter is likely pump.fun's official app, live since October 2024. The malicious Padre Terminal app has since been removed from the App Store, with its listing now returning a 404 error. Iris told BleepingComputer it suspects the trading interface of the fake app is served remotely, but has not directly observed the wallet-draining screen. According to Iris, the operation has drained 27 Solana wallets since October 25, 2026, stealing approximately $23,000 in cryptocurrency. The stolen cryptocurrency was traced to the Solana address 3LAgKYoNenWrGWT3U4XWhpgVJWyYkP9wKpiPk8TJT1LN . Iris says the attacker converted all remaining USDC (4,070 tokens) into SOL on October 29, eliminating the possibility of Circle freezing those funds. The attacker then transferred 192 SOL to a new wallet ( H84yazsUVCF8eJ6brh27rURMHjdKEVv2BuLS4iuUUQbu ). According to Iris, the two wallets held a combined 229.66 SOL, with no funds cashed out at the time of the researcher's update. The drainer remained active after the app's removal, with the latest reported theft occurring at 17:06 UTC on October 29. Iris identified at least five suspected crypto-brand impersonators on the App Store, including Padre Terminal, Axiom Pro: Focus, GMGN AI, HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools, and Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs. Their listings feature seemingly harmless descriptions, but user reviews below sometimes reveal their true nature, with many exposing them for wallet theft and scams. The Axiom Pro: Focus app, for example, had approximately 25 user reviews alleging wallet theft since February. One reviewer claimed the app had presented itself as a meme coin trading platform before changing into a focus application. A review of the GMGN AI app alleged that $2,000 had been stolen, while a review associated with HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools reported the theft of $2,020. Another app, Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs, presented itself as a notes application but had a review explicitly accusing it of stealing cryptocurrency. Iris also found a script on the fake Axiom website containing backend addresses associated with Axiom, Aster, and GMGN impersonators, suggesting a common operator. However, Padre Terminal was not linked to that cluster. Also, a script on the GMGN website blocks visitors from several CIS countries, potentially indicating that the attackers are attempting to avoid targeting users in those regions. Iris has not independently confirmed cryptocurrency theft for the four suspicious apps. BleepingComputer has contacted Apple about the Padre drainer and the other four suspicious apps available in the App Store. The company said it removed all of them from the official marketplace and will terminate the developer accounts associated with them. item.title: Hackers exploit Cisco SD-WAN flaw to deploy custom KeyDrift malware
item.description: A newly identified advanced persistent threat (APT) group tracked as UAT-11473 was observed exploiting CVE-2026-20127, an authentication-bypass flaw in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers, to deploy a custom malware framework called KeyDrift. CVE-2026-20127 is a max-severity flaw that Cisco patched in February 2026, which allows remote attackers to gain privileged access to Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager and add rogue peers. UAT-8616 has exploited the vulnerability as a zero-day since at least 2023 , and recent research also linked its exploitation to the Chinese Volt Typhoon state-sponsored hacking group. According to Cisco Talos researchers who reported on the activity, the UAT-11473 threat cluster appears to overlap with Volt Typhoon's "Silent Train" covert access network, but they made no definitive links. In a report Lumen released yesterday, researchers revealed that the Silent Train framework allowed Volt Typhoon to evade detection while conducting zero-day vulnerability attacks. The attacks Cisco researchers observed targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research organizations, using the KeyDrift malware, which is a custom malware framework designed to operate on Cisco SD-WAN controller instances. "Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material," explained Cisco Talos . "KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records." KeyDrift has two primary components, PolyFlame and LittleFilch, for which Talos saw signs of ongoing development, including new anti-debugging mechanisms and varied process impersonation. PolyFlame runs inside legitimate vdaemon processes using modified service startup scripts and an injector for deployment. It supports command execution through a TinyShell-styled component, file uploads and downloads, and relaying communications between an attacker's command-and-control (C2) server and multiple peers. LittleFilch is a control-session interception module that hooks SSL_read to inspect control-plane messages after they have been decrypted inside the controller. For predefined edge nodes, it extracts IP identifiers and a 32-byte field that Talos assesses to be AES-256 IPsec data-plane key material. It uses RSA encryption to protect the collected information, saves it to /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, and then transmits it over UDP to the attackers. Talos believes with high confidence that KeyDrift is designed to maintain persistent access to Cisco SD-WAN controllers, intercept control-plane traffic, extract cryptographic keys, and securely stage or exfiltrate the stolen data. Cisco recommends that system administrators apply the available security updates for CVE-2026-20127 and also consult the vendor's dedicated hardening guide for Catalyst SD-WAN deployments. item.title: Chrome extensions with 13.4 million installs caught hijacking searches
item.description: A massive search-hijacking campaign involving 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million reported installations redirected users' searches through tracking servers to generate advertising revenue from Bing and Yahoo. A new report by Socket's John Tuckner expands on the researcher's April 2025 discovery of 57 Chrome extensions with 6 million users, adding 264 newly identified add-ons with another 8.7 million users. "These extensions were created by a handful of organized operators all working from the same idea: quietly take over the browser's default search engine, route every query through a suspicious proxy server, and collect partner referral payments from Yahoo or Bing under a syndication partner ID," explained Tuckner . The extensions, with the full list shared at the bottom of Socket's report, pretend to be PDF converters, manual finders, safe search, and AI search tools. However, for the most part, the extensions simply redirect users' searches through a series of sites until they land on Bing or Yahoo. Although they are hosted on the Chrome Web Store, Google's official portal for Chrome add-ons, Socket says they are unlisted and don't appear in users' searches on the extension store. Instead, the extensions are promoted through shady advertisements found on websites. Tuckner explains that many of these extensions need almost no code to achieve their goal, as Chrome's built-in 'chrome_settings_overrides' setting allows them to replace the default search provider. One example analyzed in the report includes only a manifest and icons, with no background scripts, content scripts, or requested permissions. Browser-hijacking extensions like these have long blurred the line between potentially unwanted programs (PUPs) and malware, with BleepingComputer reporting on hundreds of similar extensions over the years. The extensions currently focus on revenue generation through search referrals, passing user searches through an operator-controlled server before they reach Yahoo or Bing. However, Tuckner warns that the final destination can change at any time without updating the extension, including redirecting users to phishing sites or malicious downloads. "The search referral revenue is a profitable watering hole while the proxy operator can wait for data to accumulate and targets to surface before redirecting to malicious search results or landing pages for phishing or other malicious downloads," explains Tuckner. An example of this is the Predator Search extension, which redirected Tuckner to four different sites when performing six identical searches. "Six identical searches sent through its proxy search server ended in four different places: straight to Yahoo with partner tags (hspart=sz&hsimp=yhs-026), a landing page on searchlio.net, a hop through searchtosearch.com to a second results domain (mcftink.com) before Yahoo, and a Cloudflare non-responsive error page," Tuckner reported. "The extension never changed; the proxy chose each destination as the search came in." The largest recently active cluster of extensions is "Bing-Search," with 37 extensions and 2.2 million users, often promoted through Bidbrain ads. Another one is the "SecuryBrowse" wave, with 58 extensions and 4.9 million users, promoting security-themed add-ons like Fire Shield, Securify, and WatchTower. The researcher said most of these extensions had been removed from the Chrome Web Store when the report was published. However, new ones are constantly being added. Users should uninstall the extensions listed in Socket's report from their web browsers, run a full AV scan on their systems, and avoid downloading unnecessary tools and browser add-ons from unknown publishers. BleepingComputer has contacted Google for a comment on Socket's findings, but we have not received a response by publication. item.title: 3 Ways AI Agents Already Operate in Your Browser
item.description: Which AI agents can act inside your employees' browsers today? If an agent started browsing this morning, would you know it wasn't the employee? Most security teams can't answer those questions yet. That's not a failure of effort. It's a sign of how quickly AI moved from answering questions to taking action. AI agents now operate browsers inside authenticated applications, and they get there in different ways: debugging interfaces, extensions, agentic browsers, and emerging standards like WebMCP. Each changes what an agent can access, how its actions are attributed, and whether existing controls can see them. One way AI agents operate browsers isn't new at all. It's the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). CDP was built to help developers inspect, debug, and automate Chromium-based browsers. It provides programmatic access to navigation, page content, network activity, and user interactions. Tools like Playwright and Puppeteer have used it for years. AI agents use the same approach to navigate websites, extract information, fill forms, and interact with web applications. The key distinction: automation doesn't have to originate inside the browser. An external application can connect to a browser with debugging enabled and control its tabs. If that browser has authenticated sessions, the automation can use that access. To most security tools, a browser launched with debugging enabled and signed into corporate applications looks like any other authenticated browser session. The question to ask: Which applications can launch or connect to debuggable browsers? Do your policies permit this, and which corporate sessions can those applications access? The second approach puts the agent directly inside the browser. Extensions such as Claude in Chrome can read pages, switch tabs, click buttons, and complete multistep workflows. This requires powerful permissions, including scripting, tab access, and the debugger API. These permissions enable the functionality but also expand what the extension can access. Agentic browsers like Perplexity Comet and ChatGPT Desktop go further, building AI directly into the browsing experience. These capabilities aren't necessarily governed by extension permissions, so existing extension controls may not apply. Without an inventory of browsers across your fleet, you may not know which agents are operating. Two risks stand out. Agents act with the user's identity. When an agent downloads a document or changes an internal application setting, the application sees an authenticated user making an authorized request. Without additional telemetry, neither the application nor its audit logs may distinguish the agent's actions from the employee's. Agents treat content as input. A browser displays a page for someone to interpret. An agent reads that page and decides what to do next. This introduces prompt injection risks, where instructions embedded in websites, documents, or emails attempt to redirect its behavior. The result is software interpreting untrusted content while operating with trusted permissions. The question to ask: Which AI extensions and agentic browsers are running across your fleet, what access do they have, and can you distinguish their actions from an employee's? Once an AI agent is inside an authenticated tab, endpoint and network tools lose sight of what it reads and does. Keep Aware monitors AI activity in the browser and enforces data protection policies before sensitive data leaves the tab. The third approach changes how websites interact with agents. WebMCP is an emerging web standard developed through the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group, with contributions from Google and Microsoft. item.title: CISA warns of Fragnesia Linux flaw chained in PHP2Shell attacks
item.description: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies to patch a high-severity Linux kernel privilege escalation bug that attackers are chaining with the PHP2Shell flaws in the wild. Tracked as CVE-2026-46300 and known as Fragnesia , this vulnerability stems from a logic bug in the Linux XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that lets attackers run malicious code with root permissions. Fragnesia belongs to the Dirty Frag vulnerability class and has a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit that local attackers can use to gain root privileges on major Linux distributions with kernels released before May 13, 2026. CISA added CVE-2026-46300 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Wednesday and ordered federal agencies to patch their systems by Saturday 10, as mandated by its Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. The cybersecurity agency didn't share details about ongoing Fragnesia attacks, but it noted that threat actors could chain it with two critical PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively tracked as PHP2Shell, to deploy webshells on unpatched systems. "This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root," CISA said . While CISA didn't provide more information on attackers chaining the Fragnesia and PHP2Shell flaws, Dream Security analysts said in a Monday report that the vulnerabilities were used to breach more than two dozen servers, including three belonging to a US government-affiliated organization. "Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts," they said . "This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. item.title: New Cisco firewall zero-day exploited to crash SSL VPN devices
item.description: Cisco released security updates to patch a denial-of-service zero-day in Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Threat Defense (FTD) software that attackers are exploiting to remotely crash vulnerable firewall devices. Tracked as CVE-2026-76418 , this high-severity vulnerability affects devices running ASA and FTD software with configurations containing the 'webvpn' keyword and SSL VPN enabled on at least one interface. Successful exploitation allows unauthenticated, remote attackers to trigger a denial-of-service (DoS) condition, causing the device to reload unexpectedly. Cisco advised customers to patch vulnerable firewalls after its Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) discovered evidence that the flaw was being exploited in the wild earlier this month. However, the company didn't provide indicators of compromise and hasn't shared additional information about the attacks, including which organizations are being targeted or who is exploiting the flaw. "This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition," Cisco said . "In October 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability. Cisco strongly recommends that customers upgrade to a fixed software release to remediate this vulnerability." While Cisco provided no workarounds that address this security issue, admins who can't immediately patch CVE-2026-76418 can mitigate it by disabling secondary authentication on the default DefaultWEBVPNGroup tunnel group or on any user-configured tunnel group list. Currently, Internet monitoring platform Shadowserver tracks more than 51,000 Cisco ASA SSL VPN devices exposed online, but doesn't provide information on how many have already been secured or are honeypots. ​Last year, Cisco patched two other flaws (CVE-2025-20362 and CVE-2025-20333) affecting ASA and FTD firewall devices in September and cautioned customers that attackers had exploited them in zero-day attacks targeting 5500-X Series devices with VPN web services enabled. The same day, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued Emergency Directive 25-03 , ordering federal agencies to secure their Cisco firewall devices within 24 hours. Cisco linked the attacks to the ArcaneDoor campaign , which had also been exploiting two other zero-days (CVE-2024-20353 and CVE-2024-20359) to breach government networks since November 2023. More recently, in August, Cisco addressed another denial-of-service zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2026-20349) that attackers were actively exploiting in the wild to crash affected ASA and FTD firewall devices with SSL listen sockets enabled. Earlier this month, it also warned customers to patch an actively exploited zero-day (CVE-2026-76519) in its Secure Email Gateway (SEG) security solution that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands remotely with root privileges. Since November 2021, CISA has flagged 101 Cisco security flaws as exploited in the wild, seven of which were also abused by ransomware gangs. item.title: Police seize Virtualine bulletproof service tied to ransowmare, cybercrime
item.description: U.S. law enforcement has seized the primary domain of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service advertised on cybercrime forums for facilitating illegal activities. The service also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, and promised to shield customers from legal complaints and requests from law enforcement and other authorities. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) confirmed that Virtualine marketed services that permitted "illegal/black hat activities" ranging from phishing, spamming, and carding to port scanning. The FBI seized the primary domain of the service, virtualine[.net], following an investigation that involved Germany's Polizei Hessen, the Netherlands' Politie Midden-Nederland, the U.K.'s National Crime Agency, as well as private partners OverRIPE and Lumen. Although Virtualine drew an apparent line at child content, authorities say that the operator knowingly hosted an online forum promoting child abuse material and ignored repeated notices from law enforcement, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and a victim's attorney. Authorities allege that after legal pressure against the forum increased, Virtualine worked with the administrators to set up a new site. "Virtualine hosts this new website to this day, and it has already received at least one abuse complaint about sexually explicit images of children found on that website," the DoJ said . The administrator of the Virtualine rejected the allegation in an open letter to authorities published on a new website, virtualine[.]org, captured by cybersecurity company Silent Push . The operator said that while claims about the service's illegal activities and customers "deserve a fair investigation," they regarded "sexual exploitation of children as a crime against humanity." Virtualine also accepted direct Bitcoin payments from customers, helping cybercriminals launder proceeds stolen elsewhere. Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, which provided intelligence support to law enforcement, linked Virtualine's payment addresses directly to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, scams, and phishing platforms. "Virtualine accepted direct bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without flagging their funds through hosted exchange compliance programs," Chainalysis notes . "Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin," the blockchain company added. In a report published today, blockchain intelligence firm TRM said ransomware groups were responsible for 5% of Virtualine's financial flows, while a Russian drug marketplace made up approximately 44%. "A large sextortion scheme and a mixer were also major sources of funds," the company said. TRM says that Virtualine also received payments from the StealC infostealer this year, with transactions indicating a constant financial relationship. A press release from the Dutch police notes that dozens of physical servers were seized in Limburg , taking hundreds of virtual servers offline. Politie also said its investigators recovered data from more than 3,000 Virtualine customers, and follow-up action against them is underway. According to the authorities in the Netherlands, the illegal platform was facilitating cybercrime operations since at least 2022, including ransomware, botnets, infostealers, phishing, and distribution of child abuse material. Although the bulletproof hosting provider remains partially online, researchers observed that its network prefixes currently have very low routing visibility, suggesting that much of its infrastructure may no longer be reachable.
