item.title: Discord to let search engines index public server messages
item.description: Discord will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation. The goal is to surface useful information to the wider internet community instead of keeping it buried in Discord conversations. "Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you're looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord," the messaging platform explains . The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers, publicly listed communities with at least 1,000 members. The platform says it hosts approximately 63,000 such servers. This decision excludes private servers, direct messages between users, and group announcements on servers that don't meet the requirements. According to the company's schedule, the rollout will happen in two stages: Server Web Pages will be automatically created on November 16 if admins haven't created them by then, and the only way to avoid them is to change the server type to private before the cutoff date. Discord has been piloting Community Messages and Server Web Pages in the NBA 2K, Rust, and Dead by Daylight gaming groups. The December rollout will be gradual, and Discord says messages posted before the release date will be excluded. Channel administrators can choose to exclude individual channels or turn off all channel content sharing entirely using controls available under Server Settings > Web Presence . Community members can also control if their messages appear on the Server Web Page through User Settings > Data and Privacy . However, changing that setting only affects future messages, and past messages that became public cannot be retracted. If admins and users leave the settings at their defaults, their content will automatically be included in the new sharing scheme. However, message sharing will stay off by default in all EU countries, the UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea. In those places, members must explicitly enable it in their privacy settings. Underage users are automatically excluded and cannot activate the feature until they turn 18. item.title: Sony ISP subsidiary data breach exposes 2.5 million customer records
item.description: Sony Network Communications has confirmed a data breach that compromised approximately 2.5 million records containing current and former customers' personal information. A Sony Group Corporation subsidiary, the company provides telecommunications and technology services, acting as an internet service provider (ISP) in Japan. The breach occurred on October 19 and was detected four days later, when the company shut down the compromised servers and blocked external communication. In an announcement yesterday , the company said that its So-net member database, supporting its internet access service, was accessed by an unauthorized party. The investigation confirmed that a total of 2,585,481 customer records had been exposed, including the following types of information: No banking, payment card, or other account details were exposed. An additional 54,401 email addresses from several email services were also exposed along with account passwords. The company advises users to change their passwords. In the breakdown of exposed records, Sony Network Communications says there are 2,141,986 So-net entries and 443,495 plala (S Course) records. The latter impacts another internet service provider, NTT Docomo, which contracts Sony Network Communications to provide its Docomo Hikari services. NTT Docomo also notified customers about the breach and warned of phishing emails and fake websites impersonating its d POINT Club and a Universal Studios Japan (USJ) campaign, falsely claiming that recipients had won and prompting them to enter personal information to claim tickets. Docomo says the incident affects all current Hikari service clients and those who canceled within the preceding six months. Sony reported the incident to Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission and is investigating its cause and scope. As of October 27, neither company had confirmed misuse of the exposed data in the wild. Since the start of the year, multiple cyberattacks have targeted high-value companies and providers in Japan. One of the most recent is the incident at GMO Internet Group and its Onamae Desktop Cloud service, which suffered a widespread malware attack on customer servers . Telecommunications giant KDDI suffered a breach affecting 12 million customers, and IDC Frontier was targeted by ransomware . Previously, NTT was hit in early 2025 by hackers who gained access to its systems and stole the data of 18,000 corporate customers . The recent rate of data breaches is so unprecedented and threatening that the Japanese government held urgent meetings on Monday to plan its response. item.title: Volt Typhoon hides zero-day attacks using 'Silent Train' framework
item.description: Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including for zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems. The framework has been dubbed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation, and refreshes it continuously. Researchers at Black Lotus Labs, the threat research division of communications company Lumen, have been tracking Silent Train for three years and confirmed that Volt Typhoon exploited at least four zero-day vulnerabilities in attacks targeting edge and management infrastructure. Targets include telecommunication firms, government agencies, defense contractors, educational institutes, utilities/critical infrastructure, satellite service providers, IT firms, MSPs, transportation, aviation, and emergency services. Black Lotus Labs' observations indicate the most targeted regions are California, Texas, and Hawaii, suggesting a focus on Indo-Pacific matters. Volt Typhoon previously targeted U.S. critical infrastructure, including communications, energy, transportation, and water systems, with CISA warning that it seeks to establish access for potential disruption during a future crisis or conflict. According to the researchers, Silent Train's deployment was partly fueled by the FBI's disruption of KV-Botnet , a botnet that Volt Typhoon used to evade detection when attacking critical infrastructure in the US. Silent Train is practically a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices that Volt Typhoon uses to hide the origin of its attacks. The operators route their activity through VPS infrastructure outside the United States, then pass it through hacked devices such as routers that act as intermediate relays before launching attacks. Black Lotus Labs says Intelbras modems served as overseas relays, while Netgear Orbi devices acted as hops in the U.S. The threat actor's use of Silent Train involves exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, exfiltrating data, and maintaining persistent remote access to compromised systems. By monitoring Silent Train activity, the researchers were able to observe zero-day exploits for the following products: Compromising these platforms gives threat actors broad administrative control, enabling credential theft, remote access, and reach into downstream customers without the "noisy" lateral movement that might trigger detection. "To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node," Black Lotus Labs explains in a report today. "This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and "live off the land" utilities." After the session ends, typically in under 8 hours, the threat actors remove all their tooling, keys, and configuration files from the disposable relays. By early 2025, researchers noticed that the framework become hybrid, using disposable relays alongside compromised enterprise systems thaat were retained between one and three months. Black Lotus Labs believes Silent Train was reserved for high-value targets and careful, hands-on operations conducted on China Standard Time (CST) timezone. The use of zero-days against those targets further strengthens the assumption. The researchers recommend strengthening security around centralized management systems, restricting internet access to administrative interfaces, rapidly patching vulnerabilities, and centralizing logs with longer retention. They also advise monitoring for unusual administrative activity, reviewing trusted connections that could expose customer or partner networks, and following CISA and NCSC guidance on Volt Typhoon. item.title: Microsoft urges Entra ID admins to migrate users to passkeys
item.description: Microsoft again asked Entra ID administrators to migrate users to phishing-resistant methods to avoid sign-in disruptions before it retires SMS and voice authentication in February 2027. This retirement process applies only to Microsoft Entra ID workforce tenant authentication scenarios and not to Azure AD B2C or Microsoft Entra External ID customer identity scenarios. Before Microsoft retires SMS and voice authentication, admins should ensure all users in their organizations use a phishing-resistant method, since they will no longer be able to use them to complete multifactor authentication and log in to their accounts. Admins can choose from passkeys, QR code authentication, FIDO2 security keys, and other Entra ID-supported sign-in methods. "Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication will retire starting February 1, 2027. Complete your migration before rollout begins to avoid interrupting users' sign-in experience," Microsoft said in a Microsoft 365 Message Center update on Tuesday. "SMS and voice are vulnerable to phishing and SIM-swap attacks. Microsoft recommends passkeys for stronger, phishing-resistant protection. You can also migrate to another supported authentication method or retain SMS and voice by configuring a customer-managed telecom provider (CYOT) through the Microsoft Security Store." As Microsoft noted in a previous reminder issued in September, admins with the Authentication Policy Administrator, Global Reader, or Security Reader roles can find users with SMS or voice authentication with the Entra SMS/Voice Policy Scanner PowerShell script . Organizations that must use phone-based authentication have to configure third-party telecom providers through the Microsoft Security Store. In July, Microsoft announced that passkeys will start rolling out as the default authentication experience for the Entra ID enterprise identity service starting in September. "As the rollout reaches each organization, users enabled for SMS or voice authentication will automatically be enabled for passkeys, and the next time they perform multifactor authentication, they'll be prompted to register a passkey," Microsoft said . "Following this transition, on February 1, 2027, Microsoft will retire Microsoft-provided telecom delivery for SMS and voice authentication and will no longer offer SMS and voice as a native Microsoft Entra capability." Microsoft also retired SMS first-factor sign-in for Microsoft Entra ID Free tenants in August due to phishing, fraud, and account compromise risks, and stopped enabling it for newly created tenants. item.title: InfraTrust report warns of exploited flaws in critical network infrastructure
item.description: Attackers are actively exploiting vulnerabilities across critical network infrastructure, and PHP flaws known as "PHP2Shell" put the web management interfaces of firewalls, VPNs, application delivery controllers, and other appliances at risk. The findings come from Eclypsium's October InfraTrust Pulse , a monthly report tracking security advisories affecting network devices, servers, firmware, chips, and other infrastructure. Between September 18 and October 14, InfraTrust tracked 133 new security advisories across 18 vendors, covering 2,813 vulnerabilities. Of those advisories, 37 were rated critical, five had a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and 58 could be exploited remotely without authentication. Sixteen newly published advisories included vulnerabilities listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (KEV) as they were actively exploited. The report also warns that many network appliances, including firewalls, VPN gateways, application delivery controllers, and network-attached storage devices, embed PHP into their management interfaces. Because vendors compile PHP into appliance firmware, customers commonly cannot install the recent PHP security updates themselves and must instead wait for each vendor to release updated firmware. InfraTrust therefore recommends that administrators make sure PHP-backed management interfaces are not exposed to the Internet while waiting for PHP2Shell patches. Some of the most serious vulnerabilities affect systems at the edge of enterprise networks or used to manage other infrastructure. Threat actors target these devices because they can provide initial access to corporate environments or serve as a springboard for further attacks. Among the actively exploited flaws highlighted by InfraTrust are: InfraTrust also warns that the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities expose another weakness in network infrastructure, as many appliances embed PHP directly into their management interfaces. The two PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, allow unauthenticated remote code execution, and the PHP project fixed them on October 21. While most focus on these vulnerabilities has been on websites and web applications written in PHP, PHP is also used for management interfaces of firewalls, application delivery controllers, VPN appliances, and network-attached storage devices. For impacted devices, administrators usually cannot update PHP themselves because vendors compile it directly into the appliance firmware. Instead, customers must wait for each vendor to rebuild and release updated firmware or software containing the patched PHP version. Soon after the disclosure, Palo Alto Networks, F5, NetScaler, Check Point, and QNAP confirmed that some of their products were affected, while they still developed fixes for appliances. The report also highlights a similar issue in other software components that infrastructure vendors bundle into their products. CVE-2026-31431, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw known as Copy Fail , has now appeared in 29 advisories across eight vendors, up from 19 advisories from six vendors last month. InfraTrust also found older, exploited vulnerabilities in bundled components, including an Android kernel flaw affecting HP LaserJet Enterprise printers and a 2020 jQuery vulnerability in Dell Data Lakehouse software. InfraTrust recommends that administrators prioritize patching NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure because these remote-access gateways can serve as a doorway into corporate networks. Next, it recommends Fortinet's October 22 FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer security updates for internet-facing devices. The report then recommends focusing on Check Point Security Management Server, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, VeloCloud Orchestrator, FortiMail, Cisco Secure Email Gateway, affected BIG-IP APM systems, and PAN-OS management interfaces. item.description: Here's a prediction: we're about to see a stellar quarter for application security companies. PHP2Shell is about to become the strongest budget argument application security vendors have had in years. AI helped researchers find two remote code execution vulnerabilities in the language behind 69% of the web , attackers targeted it before the patch shipped, and the pitch writes itself: find more bugs and fix them faster. Enterprises should rethink this idea. Security teams cannot patch at machine speed, but they can reduce what an attacker can reach after exploitation by focusing on identity as the control plane. Beyond the initial exploitation, the ultimate incident severity depends heavily on which service accounts, API keys, cloud roles, and tokens the compromised workload can use and what they can access. First, we need to understand just how much faster exploitation is now. The two flaws behind PHP2Shell had been in PHP's code since 2012 . Researchers at Calif and Wiz found them in August, with help from OpenAI and Google models, and disclosed them jointly with OpenAI. Amazon saw an exploitation attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure. PHP shipped the patch on October 21, and watchTowr saw exploitation attempts in the wild the same day. Cloudflare observed attack traffic escalating rapidly after disclosure, and on October 26, CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities. Exploitation now often starts before disclosure. Unfortunately, things aren't moving as quickly on the remediation side. Verizon's 2026 DBIR states the median time-to-fix of a known exploited vulnerability is 43 days. According to Qualys , the mean remediation time is 21.2 days, and 63% of critical vulnerabilities are still open after a week. All while around 195 new CVEs are published every day. PHP2Shell will take longer than most to clean up. PHP ships inside appliances and hosting control panels that customers can't patch themselves. Moreover, versions 8.1 and older got no official builds. As of October 27, Censys counted 32.5 million internet-facing PHP services still running potentially vulnerable versions, and more than 60 million others that don't report a version at all. However you look at it, remediation speed will remain slower than the pace of exploitation for the foreseeable future, even when patching itself benefits greatly from AI-driven workflows. Agents now act across your systems with access nobody has reviewed. Token Security's AI Agent Security finds every agent, links it to an owner, and limits what it can do. item.title: Hackers now scanning systems for recently-patched Oracle flaw
item.description: Attackers have begun probing the Internet for systems unpatched against a recently disclosed critical Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS) vulnerability. Discovered in a core component of EBS's Application Object Library and tracked as CVE-2026-101767 , this flaw lets unauthenticated threat actors with HTTP network access take over vulnerable systems in low-complexity attacks. Oracle released security updates to address the issue in its October 2026 Critical Security Patch Update on October 20 and urged customers to patch their systems immediately. "In some instances, it has been reported that attackers have been successful because targeted customers had failed to apply available Oracle patches," it said. "Oracle therefore strongly recommends that customers remain on actively-supported versions and apply security patches without delay." While Oracle has not yet tagged CVE-2026-101767 as exploited in the wild, threat intelligence company Defused said on Tuesday that it already spotted threat actors scanning the Internet for vulnerable systems. "Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27," Defused warned . ​Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 670 Internet-exposed Oracle EBS instances , most of them with IP addresses from the United States. However, Shadowserver doesn't indicate how many are honeypots or have already been secured against the CVE-2026-101767 flaw. ​Attackers often target Oracle vulnerabilities because they let them breach enterprise systems on the networks of many Fortune 100 corporations, government organizations, and healthcare networks around the world. For instance, since early August 2025 , the Clop extortion gang has exploited another Oracle EBS flaw (CVE-2025-61882) in zero-day attacks targeting high-profile victims like Logitech , GlobalLogic , and the Washington Post , as well as US universities (including Harvard University , the University of Pennsylvania , Dartmouth College , and the University of Phoenix ) More recently, in June, Oracle released emergency mitigations for a critical PeopleSoft Suite zero-day (CVE-2026-35273) that the ShinyHunters extortion gang exploited between May 27 and June 9 . By abusing this flaw, the threat actors gained unauthenticated remote code execution on victims' systems and stole data from many organizations worldwide, including Nottingham University , Nissan , and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) . Since November 2021, CISA has added 46 Oracle security bugs to its list of actively exploited vulnerabilities, 13 of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks. item.title: CISA warns of hackers now exploiting critical Node2Shell flaw
item.description: On Tuesday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed that hackers have begun exploiting a critical Brotli vulnerability known as Node2Shell , Broccoli2Shell , and HTTP2Shell . Tracked as CVE-2026-111497 , this critical-severity flaw stems from an out-of-bounds write weakness in the Brotli decoder used to expand data compressed with Google's widely popular Brotli lossless compression algorithm. Unprivileged attackers can use a maliciously crafted Brotli-compressed stream to trigger crashes or memory leaks and, in some cases, gain remote code execution on devices with vulnerable Brotli libraries or binaries. The security issue was first identified in the Node.js JavaScript runtime environment, but it also affects HTTP servers and clients that rely on vulnerable Brotli implementations. On Sunday, Microsoft also pushed an emergency .NET security update , warning that attackers could exploit it to escalate privileges on systems with a vulnerable .NET version. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Tuesday and ordered US government agencies to patch their systems within two weeks, by November 10, as mandated by its Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. "Google Brotli contains an unchecked return value vulnerability that allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream," it said. "These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise." While CISA's BOD 26-04 applies only to federal agencies, the cybersecurity agency urged all network defenders to prioritize patching this security flaw to block incoming attacks. Security teams that can't apply the updates immediately should block incoming Brotli-compressed requests at the proxy or firewall level, or disable the Brotli decoding feature until they can update. After patching, administrators must also restart affected processes and rebuild and redeploy affected container images. item.title: Nefilim and Hive ransomware affiliate gets 70 months in prison
item.description: A Ukrainian national was sentenced to 70 months in prison for his role in Nefilim and Hive ransomware attacks targeting hospitals, government entities, and high-revenue businesses worldwide between 2018 and 2021. The sentence follows the extradition of 35-year-old Artem Aleksandrovych Stryzhak to the United States on April 30, 2025, after authorities arrested him in Spain in June 2024. "Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals," said Brett Leatherman, the FBI's Cyber Branch Operations Director. "These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today's sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak's crimes and demonstrates the FBI's global reach and extensive network of international partners." According to court documents, he paid for 20% of all ransom payments collected for access to custom Nefilim ransomware and decryption keys starting in June 2021. While active as a Nefilim affiliate until October 2021, Stryzhak used the custom-tailored malware to target large corporations in the United States, Canada, and Australia with revenues exceeding $100 million each year. However, one of the Nefilim administrators later encouraged him to focus on large companies that were generating more than $200 million annually. To pressure victims into paying, the ransomware operation also threatened to leak data stolen during attacks on dark web "Corporate Leaks" websites managed by the Nefilim admins unless victims met the ransom demands. ​Stryzhak also joined Hive ransomware as an early affiliate, breaching and encrypting the systems of seven victims, including a dentist's office, multiple law firms, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. In December 2025, Stryzhak pleaded guilty and admitted to computer fraud conspiracy charges brought by US prosecutors in connection with ransomware attacks targeting businesses in the United States, Norway, France, Switzerland, Germany, and the Netherlands. "Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office," added US Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe. "Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors," US Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. noted. The US State Department also offers up to $11 million for any details that could lead to the arrest of Ukrainian national Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, one of Stryzhak's alleged accomplices, who is still at large. Tymoshchuk is on the most-wanted lists of the European Union and the FBI , and the US Justice Department charged him in September for his roles as an administrator for the LockerGoga, MegaCortex, and Nefilim ransomware gangs. item.title: Japan's GMO urges customers to shut down PCs amid ransomware threat
item.description: The GMO Group has urged customers to disconnect their systems from the internet and shut down computers after a threat actor who breached the company's Onamae Desktop Cloud threatened to launch a ransomware attack today. The company later confirmed that data belonging to both the company and its customers had been published online. The alert concerns a cyberattack on Onamae Desktop Cloud , a popular VPS provider in Japan operated by GMO Internet, a member of GMO Internet Group and one of Japan's largest domain registrars. Last week, the company announced it detected an intrusion on October 20 that could have installed malware on up to 26,739 customers' servers. To minimize the risk, the company shut down the servers and reduced service availability before launching an investigation. The internet company assured customers that their payment information had not been exposed but warned that MetaTrader 4 and MetaTrader 5 (MT4/MT5) credentials and trading-account details may have been exposed or compromised. It urged customers to reset their passwords and terminate active sessions. Subsequent updates from the company confirmed that data had been stolen and that the attacker was demanding a ransom of ¥8 billion ($50 million), which GMO said it would not pay. Instead, the company announced it would compensate each customer ¥5,000 ($30) for the inconvenience caused. On October 26, GMO warned that threat actors planned to leak customer information online and trigger a ransomware payload planted on customer servers earlier in the attack. The next day, the company asked customers to disconnect their PCs from the internet, shut them down, and unplug all cables before noon, while it worked with Trend Micro to recover from the cyberattack. "Once you have a backup, disconnect the network, power it down, and unplug the cord that connects to your PC," advised GMO to customers. The company said it was scanning customer systems to determine whether malware was still present, and offered equivalent PC replacements to those who suffered damages from a ransomware attack. In a report published earlier today, GMO confirmed that the threat actor had published company and customer data , prompting efforts to verify the authenticity of the leaked information. For customers whose information was exposed, GMO said it will consider additional financial compensation. It appears that the attacker never acted on their threat, as no ransomware was activated on customer machines. The company warned people and the media not to disseminate the exposed information, announcing it will take legal action against those who do, while reaffirming its refusal to pay the attackers. item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra is safer overall, but shows more destructive-action flags in tests
item.description: OpenAI confirmed GPT-6.1 Terra is safer overall than some of its older models, but its safety testing also found other problems. According to OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Terra showed higher rates of exfiltration, destructive actions, and attempts to bypass restrictions than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI performed simulations across approximately 48,690 matched tasks and found that Terra received 22 severity-3-or-higher flags, or 0.045%. For comparison, GPT-6 Sol received 38, while GPT-5.6 Sol received 61. "GPT-6.1 Terra received approximately 42% fewer severity level 3 or higher flags than GPT-6 Sol and 64% fewer than GPT-5.6 Sol," OpenAI noted in its system card . However, that is no longer the case when you compare Terra with other newer models on less severe behaviors. "Relative to GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, we observed higher rates of flags for concealing uncertainty, circumventing restrictions, exfiltration, other misalignment, destructive action and inbound prompt injection," OpenAI explained. Terra is clearly safer overall, but we can't overlook the other potential security issues it has, and this is true for all models shipping in the market, including Claude. OpenAI also tested what happens when Terra needs to deal with messages from other AI agents while working through blocked coding tasks. Terra attempted to communicate with those apparent peers in 65% of tests and ultimately performed the specified unauthorized action in 13.75%, or 11 of 80 samples. OpenAI found that GPT-6.1 Sol did so in just 1.25%. "These results indicate that performance is comparable to 6.0 Sol," OpenAI noted, adding that much of the regression against GPT-6.1 Sol involved promises of future help that Terra indicated it would not actually carry out. OpenAI warns that these tests were conducted in simulated environments, so the results may not necessarily reflect how GPT-6.1 Terra behaves in real-world production environments. But we still aren't seeing meaningful improvements across every area of security, even as these companies claim their models can control computers and code better. item.title: UNM Health ransomware attack disrupts patient care, surgeries
item.description: The University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center disclosed a cyberattack that caused system outages and disrupted patient care and academic activities. On Monday, UNM Health, the university's healthcare provider, began temporarily limiting new patient admissions, diverting ambulances to nearby hospitals, and suspending outpatient surgeries and appointments. In an update on the incident, UNM said UNM Hospital and Sandoval Regional Medical Center remain open, and all clinics will resume scheduled appointments and procedures starting today, Tuesday, October 27. Regarding emergencies, the healthcare organization advised that people should call 911. However, today's classes at its four health sciences schools are canceled, and nonessential HSC employees were instructed to stay home. UNM Health is a major statewide provider of specialist care with more than 1 million patient visits annually. Its flagship UNM Hospital in Albuquerque houses New Mexico's only Level I trauma center , treating the most seriously injured patients. UNM did not disclose the type of cyberattack it suffered, but BleepingComputer found that a new ransomware group called Byod had claimed the attack. In a post on their data leak site, the threat actor said it had compromised 36,000 systems across UNM's main campus and hospital environments, including Active Directory forests, Group Policy infrastructure, the entire Microsoft Entra tenant, and two Oracle databases. "This is your entire network and infrastructure compromised, the entire university COMPLETELY," the threat actor said. They claim access to student and employee personal data, including: In an attempt to force a payment, Byod ransomware said it would take down the breach post after the university initiated communication, likely for negotiating a ransom. BleepingComputer has reached out to UNM Health Sciences with a request for comment about these data theft allegations, but we have not received a response. In a new post today, Byod ransomware said it would provide free keys that decrypt locked systems at healthcare facilities. Furthermore, the threat actor promised to pay up to $2,500 for every patient affected by the cyberattack. "We have morals and we have a heart, we are not villains, but we will still continue to hold companies responsible for bad security leading to the compromise of any customer data," the cybercriminals said. However, the threat actor also said that it would keep all the stolen data. Byod is a new ransomware gang that currently lists six victims on its data leak site. For three of them, it has already leaked the allegedly stolen data. On its FAQ page, the threat group claims it is doing "pentesting" to expose vulnerabilities and hold data controllers accountable for breaches. Byod says no target is off-limits, but it selects victims after an initial assessment identifies a target of interest. The group says it focuses on "those at the top who look at consumers and/or customers as a number or another dollar in their pockets." The UNM Health Sciences said today that all its critical electronic systems are back online and all UNM Health hospitals are fully open. Ambulance traffic is now operating normally, and all clinics have resumed scheduled appointments and procedures. The university said the quick recovery was possible due to IT security teams working "with external partners to secure the network." "Their assessment determined that the event affected some end-user devices but did not penetrate core systems or servers," UNM Health Sciences Center notes. Patients who received care at UNM hospitals, as well as staff and students who work and study there, are advised to remain vigilant for unsolicited communications and phishing attacks. item.title: Hackers hijack Convertr analytics script to steal payment card data
item.description: A credit card skimming group reportedly compromised a shared analytics script used by e-commerce platform Convertr to steal shoppers' payment data during checkout. The campaign was identified on October 24 and has been attributed to a Brazilian gang, active since at least July 2024, that focuses on infecting online stores running Magento, OpenCart, and WooCommerce platforms. Convertr is a Brazilian e-commerce platform that powers online stores and checkout systems for dozens of major fashion brands in the country, handling R$2 billion ($370M) in sales. E-commerce security firm Sansec says that the attacker modified the Plausible tracker file hosted on a self-managed server operated by Convertr. Ecommerce cybersecurity company Sansec says that the attacker modified the tracker file on a self-hosted server for Plausible, an open source alternative to Google Analytics, managed by Convertr. Sansec suspects the attackers exploited CVE-2026-8467, an unauthenticated command-execution vulnerability affecting Convertr's outdated Plausible Community Edition installation, to gain initial access. However, this hasn't been confirmed. After gaining access, the attackers injected malicious code into a legitimate Plausible analytics tracker hosted on Convertr's infrastructure, which loads on the checkout pages of all merchants using the platform. Sansec says that earlier versions of the skimmer used generic payment-field patterns, but by October 26, the attackers pushed a more refined version that specifically targeted Convertr's exact payment API field names. The injected skimmer was configured to steal the following data types from checkout pages: The researchers suggest that those who paid by card on a Brazilian store that contained the 'checkout.convertr' string in the checkout address page since October 24 should contact their bank immediately and ask to block their card. In an update today, Sansec confirmed that Convertr "removed the skimmer and upgraded Plausible to a patched version," noting that the company announced it was notifying affected merchants and payment providers. BleepingComputer has contacted Convertr for a statement on the incident, but we have not received a response yet. Sansec researchers warned that browser caching could keep the malicious script active on impacted sites for up to 24 hours after cleanup, so customers should clear their cache before placing new orders, even after the threat has been eliminated. One way to protect payment card details when shopping online is to use disposable virtual cards that expire immediately after a transaction. item.title: Microsoft releases Windows OOB updates to distrust eMudhra certificates
item.description: Microsoft has released out-of-band (OOB) Windows updates to remove trust in certificates tied to compromised eMudhra certificate authority keys, protecting systems that do not receive automatic certificate trust updates. The KB5134133 update for Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 and the KB5134125 update for Windows 10 versions 21H2 and 22H2 were released on October 26. The updates are for systems without Internet access, devices that cannot access Microsoft's certificate-update service, and those where automatic Certificate Trust List (CTL) updates have been disabled. The updates were released after the discovery of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority private keys that were so weak they could be recovered almost instantly. All eight keys were generated in April 2025 and had values smaller than 256, allowing anyone to recover them by testing just 256 possible numbers. The compromised keys could have allowed attackers to forge certificates for legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications. After the disclosure, eMudhra revoked the eight compromised intermediate certificates, and Mozilla, Google, Apple, and other software vendors also began revoking them. In response, Microsoft previously updated the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List to block the eight affected intermediate certificate authorities, including six used for TLS and two for code signing. The company also released a CRLSet update for Microsoft Edge and WebView2 to block affected TLS certificates, which enabled the block without requiring a browser update. Microsoft is now taking further steps by removing seven certificates associated with the affected certificate hierarchies from its Windows trust list. "On October 26, Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update that removes seven certificates associated with the affected hierarchies: six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign, from the Windows trust list," Microsoft explained . The new update goes further by also removing trust in the eMudhra root certificates used to verify other certificates issued by the CA. Microsoft says the same seven certificates will also be removed from the Edge trust list on October 27. "Removing a root from a trust list is not the same as revoking the known impacted intermediate certificate authorities," explains Microsoft. "This is a separate trust decision, broader than blocking the identified compromised intermediate keys. Organizations with a specific compatibility need may choose to trust a certificate locally, subject to their own security assessment and policies." The company advises admins to install the update on disconnected Windows systems and identify any certificates that depend on the removed roots, as they may need to be replaced. Microsoft is also investigating the remaining eMudhra roots and may make additional trust changes as needed. item.title: Warp discloses breach exposing AI agent logs, user telemetry data
item.description: Agent decision logs and telemetry data belonging to Warp agentic development environment users were exposed in an attack on a third-party vendor in the project's infrastructure. The company's founder and CEO, Zach Lloyd, estimates that "roughly 1% of Warp users may have been impacted," but external experts are helping with the ongoing investigation. Warp is a popular developer tool that started as a modern terminal and evolved into an agentic development environment (ADE) that allows developers to direct AI agents to write and test code and deploy software. The environment provides a terminal, a code editor, task orchestration, and agent review tools in a single workspace. The project's website says the platform has at least 800,000 users . "On Friday, we became aware of what we believe to be an active and narrow-banded exploitation of a vendor in Warp's infrastructure," Lloyd stated . "We detected the operation within hours and were able to remediate and mitigate the impact," the CEO added. Although agent traces and telemetry were identified as potentially affected data, the company did not clarify whether the exposed information included source code, prompts, credentials, or other sensitive details. Analysis of the incident suggests that the attack was powered by "an agent swarm" that relied on "a very sophisticated penetration and escalation technique." Lloyd said that Warp has contacted the third-party vendor about the vulnerability, but no details have been shared. The platform has notified users identified to be impacted. The cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has also been engaged to assist with the investigation, while the platform has also informed law enforcement authorities. The incident at Warp follows an incident at AI coding platform OpenCode , which notified users last week that a security breach exposed stored API keys used with external providers. The incident affected a small percentage of OpenCode users, about 1.4%, and led to unauthorized charges of up to $1,700 for some. Warp users are advised to remain vigilant, monitor account activity, and treat unsolicited communications with increased caution. item.title: Tailscale warns of SSH flaws allowing root privilege escalation
item.description: The Tailscale security team is working to patch almost a dozen security vulnerabilities that could be exploited to steal credentials, crash servers, gain root privileges, and more. Tailscale develops a software-defined mesh virtual private network (VPN) built on WireGuard that lets users connect computers, servers, and cloud instances from anywhere to the same encrypted mesh network ("tailnet") via direct peer-to-peer (P2P) connections. Cyberdione Labs discovered 11 flaws (collectively known as Tailworm ) that still lack patches during a security audit of Tailscale 1.104.2 and the self-hosted headscale v0.29.5 control server. "All findings were verified by reproduction in a lab environment on unmodified, released software (tailscale v1.104.2, headscale v0.29.5)," said Erica Windisch, founder of Cyberdione Labs, who reported the flaws to Tailscale and publicly released the details. "It is the opinion of the researchers that rapid awareness of these flaws will expediate remediation across impacted devices. These vulnerabilities were not introduced by the researchers, but were discovered, and discovered with low effort." The table below classifies the security issues by the component they affect. The most critical issue is in Tailscale's SSH server and could let authorized attackers gain code execution with root privileges through Unix-socket forwarding on a targeted tailnet. On Monday, the Tailscale team said it received Cyberdione Labs' report and was working on patches to address these security issues by the end of today. The developers also confirmed that the reported flaws are "serious" as they could let threat actors with permissions on targeted systems take actions with escalated privileges. "Most of the Tailscale SSH issues we've identified concern privilege escalation. In some circumstances, someone already authorized to connect over Tailscale SSH may be able to perform actions beyond the permissions of their configured local user, including potentially gaining elevated privileges," Tailscale said . "These are serious security issues, and we're treating them accordingly. Exploitation depends on the permissions granted to the connecting user or device, the system's configuration, and other conditions. We're continuing to verify the full scope of the findings and which configurations may be affected." However, despite the severity of the issues, Tailscale said it doesn't recommend that users disable the Tailscale SSH feature. "If you want to jump to the most important part, based on our current assessment, we're not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH," said Mike Shaver, VP of Engineering at Tailscale. Instead, the Tailscale team shared measures that should mitigate some of these flaws: The Tailscale devs aim to push a new version that fixes these issues by the end of Tuesday, October 27, and urged users to prepare to update and "apply the patched Tailscale client release when it becomes available." item.title: The Huntress Tragic Quadrant: Ranking Threats Hitting Businesses Hardest
item.description: Cyber headlines often focus on the flashy attacks, but the ones that actually cause OH $#!T moments are the tactics that abuse the tools and workflows you already trust. If you run a small or mid-sized organization, whether you handle IT yourself or outsource it, it's a constant race to keep up with attackers and their evolving tactics. The bottom line is that you need to know which attacks are landing in environments like yours, and how to prioritize your defenses against them. That's why Huntress created the Tragic Quadrant , a ranked list of the cyber tactics putting businesses at risk, built to show you where to focus regardless of what's trending week to week. Each of these tactics hides inside something your team uses every day, like a remote access tool or a Microsoft 365 login. Remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools are a staple for IT teams, which is exactly why attackers abuse them. One rogue RMM install gives an attacker persistent access that looks like ordinary admin work. In Q1 2026, 45% of endpoint-related incidents Huntress investigated involved RMM abuse. Attackers are also using AI to build convincing fake document shares and service agreement lures that trick users into installing unwanted RMMs . So far in 2026, 24.6% of Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) signals point to mailbox manipulation and persistence. With mailbox access, an attacker can change inbox rules and send vendor replies to folders nobody is watching, like RSS Feeds or Archive. From there, they can tweak invoice details and redirect payments to their own accounts, all without any malware for detection tools to flag. Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks made up 18.9% of all identity-based threats Huntress tracked in 2025. The attacker sits between the victim and the real Microsoft 365 login page, steals the session token in transit, and forwards everything along so nothing looks off to the user. As long as that session is valid, the attacker can access the account without a password or a fresh MFA prompt. Your files are encrypted, your operations are down, an attacker has named their price, and they're waiting for you to respond. Do you pay? Do you negotiate? Do you even engage at all? Choose your next move in a simulated ransomware incident, built from tactics Huntress has seen used against real businesses. You'll see how ransomware operators behave when they think they're in control, and what steps you can take for catching an attack before it becomes a negotiation. Once you've covered the top-right tactics, the others still deserve a plan. Each one is evolving fast, potentially moving toward the OH $#!T corner at any time. Device code phishing is less common, but it rides on Microsoft's real device code login flow, so "check the URL" advice doesn't help. A convincing prompt nudges someone to enter a short code on a genuine Microsoft page, and the attacker walks away with an access token that can outlive a password reset. In one 16-day window, a phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit called EvilTokens hit 344 organizations across five countries. Defenders should be suspicious of unusual device code prompts and odd token activity. ClickFix leans on the copy-paste muscle memory people use to get past everyday friction. A fake CAPTCHA or "verification failed" prompt tricks someone into pasting a malicious command into their terminal. The paste itself triggers the malicious code, so no exploit chain is involved, and it can lead to infostealer malware or ransomware. ClickFix accounts for about 2.2% of Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) detection signals so far in 2026, but nearly 99% of those detections are high severity. This one sits in the overhyped corner because it's still an emerging pattern. Attackers hide malicious content behind real AI tools and workflows people trust. item.title: Apple backports CoreGraphics zero-day patches to older iPhones
item.description: ​Apple has backported security patches released last month to older iPhones and iPads, addressing a zero-day bug exploited in "extremely sophisticated" targeted attacks on iOS devices. Apple patched the same vulnerability in September for devices running iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1. Meta Product Security discovered this out-of-bounds write weakness (tracked as CVE-2026-86950 ) in CoreGraphics, a framework used for two-dimensional vector graphics, text drawing, and image rendering across iOS, macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and tvOS. Successful exploitation of out-of-bounds write security issues can let attackers crash programs, corrupt data, or gain remote code execution by writing data outside the allocated memory buffer. "Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27," Apple warned on Monday . "Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved bounds checking." With this week's security patches, Apple has now also addressed this vulnerability on iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later. While Apple said CVE-2026-86950 is exploited only in highly targeted attacks, it is strongly advised to install these backported patches to block potential attacks. With this vulnerability, Apple has fixed two zero-days exploited in attacks this year. The other (CVE-2026-20700), an arbitrary code execution vulnerability in dyld (the Dynamic Link Editor used by Apple operating systems) also exploited in "extremely sophisticated" targeted attacks, was patched in February . Earlier this year, Apple also fixed a high-severity Beats Studio Buds flaw (CVE-2025-20701) that lets attackers in Bluetooth range spy on users' conversations, and patched older iPhones and iPads against four vulnerabilities targeted in cyberespionage and crypto-theft attacks using the Coruna exploit kit. item.title: Energy giant ENGIE discloses data breach affecting customers
item.description: French energy giant ENGIE, one of the world's largest power and natural gas providers, confirmed that attackers stole customer data after breaching a marketing platform used by business partners. ENGIE operates in renewable energy, infrastructure, and customer energy supply in 30 countries, employs over 90,000 people, and reported €71.9 billion in revenue last year. An ENGIE spokesperson told BleepingComputer that it cut off the attackers' access to the compromised platform and that they didn't breach the company's internal systems. "ENGIE's internal IT systems were not compromised. ENGIE recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers," the spokesperson said. The ENGIE spokesperson didn't say how many customers were affected, but told BleepingComputer the incident is limited to customers in France. Since the attack, ENGIE has notified relevant authorities and contacted affected customers to inform them of the breach. "The investigations conducted to date indicate that the data concerned is limited to customers' contact details and certain information relating to their energy contracts. No banking data is affected," ENGIE told BleepingComputer. "In the interest of transparency, ENGIE individually informed each customer concerned and reminded them of the precautionary measures they should take to protect themselves against potential fraud or phishing attempts." Although the company didn't share what customer information was stolen in the attack, it said in breach notification letters sent to affected customers that the threat actors gained access to their first and last names, mailing address, email address, phone number, Delivery Point (PDL) or Metering and Estimation Point (PCE), customer ID, and contract number. ENGIE didn't attribute the attack to a specific threat group, and no ransomware operation or extortion gang has claimed the ENGIE breach before publication. One year ago, the Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters extortion group also leaked records they claimed to have stolen after allegedly breaching a Salesforce instance of Engie Records , the retail energy supply subsidiary of ENGIE North America. item.title: CISA confirms PHP2Shell vulnerabilities now exploited in attacks
item.description: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities collectively tracked as PHP2Shell to its catalog of actively exploited security flaws. Threat actors without privileges can exploit the two security issues (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) in high-complexity attacks to gain remote code execution (RCE) on unpatched systems. ​ The PHP security team patched the two flaws on Wednesday, October 21, one day after urging security teams to install the security updates as soon as they became available. Although details on the PHP2Shell security flaws (including the CVE IDs and mitigation measures shared with critical infrastructure providers) leaked and some proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits were published online before patches went live, the PHP security team said that none were functional. Multiple cybersecurity firms (including Cloudflare , Amazon , Hadrian , watchTowr , Previdian , and Patchstack ) also detected widespread exploitation attempts before public disclosure, but they all tagged them as unsuccessful. Amazon Threat Intelligence security researchers also said that attackers began targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities four days before security patches were released . CISA added the vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on Monday and ordered Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems by Thursday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive 26-04. "These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," the cybersecurity agency warned. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities." While CISA has not yet shared further details about ongoing PHP2Shell attacks, Perplexity detection and response lead Adel Karimi first confirmed in-the-wild exploitation over the weekend after their honeypots recorded evidence of remote code execution against an Apache mod_php installation running PHP 8.4.26. On Friday, the PHP security team also shared mitigation for a new RCE flaw (CVE-2026-115560) with no patch, exploitable when targeting systems "with an unusual combination of configuration and application code." PHP powers roughly 70% of all websites, with more than 5.1 million PHP hosts exposed online and around 3.8 million instances with at least one port open to attacks, according to VirusTotal estimates .
